n: In this lecture we will consider the topic of HIV/AIDS and autopsy. The central nervous system, that is, the CNS, is regarded in AIDS as the second most frequently affected organ after the lungs. Autopsy is a valuable method for understanding the natural course of the disease, and also for recognising infections and malignant tumours not identified clinically. However, systematic studies assessing neuropathological findings in HIV autopsies are rare. It is exactly this gap that determines the relevance of today's topic.

Today's topic rests on two studies. The first is the Brazilian study: in it, CNS changes were studied retrospectively in 284 AIDS autopsies from 1989-2008, and the method was histology. The second is the South African study: in adults with CD4 ≤150 cells/µL, 34 minimally invasive autopsies, that is, MIA, were carried out, looking for tuberculosis and other infections. That is, the first, on the basis of classical autopsy, focuses on the CNS, and the second on the minimally invasive method.

t: Opportunistic agents and tumours in the CNS
n: The most frequent opportunistic agents in the CNS are three: Toxoplasma gondii, Cryptococcus neoformans and cytomegalovirus. Among tumours, primary non-Hodgkin lymphomas predominate. Changes characteristic of HIV usually appear at the late stage of the disease. Remember: multinucleated giant cells in the CNS are considered "pathognomonic" for HIV. This means that finding such cells is assessed as a sign of the action of HIV.

After highly active antiretroviral therapy, that is, HAART, the situation changed: opportunistic infections decreased, while HIV encephalitis increased. In the rest of the world, in more than 90 % of AIDS cases, patients do not survive to the appearance of neurological complications of HIV. In developing countries such autopsy studies are even fewer. For this reason it remains difficult to determine the true prevalence of neuropathological changes.

The prevalence of tuberculous meningitis differs greatly by place. In HIV autopsies, tuberculous meningitis was observed in India in 12 % and in Africa in 11 % of cases. In the USA, however, it occurred in only 1.4 % of cases. This means that in assessing CNS findings it is necessary to take into account the region in which the study was conducted.

The clinical and pathomorphological value of autopsy is shown by two studies. Wilkes, in 101 autopsies, established that 74 % of AIDS-related diseases were not suspected clinically. Among the unsuspected, cytomegalovirus was 49 %, systemic fungi 20 %, Kaposi's sarcoma 14 %, mycobacteriosis 11 % and CNS lymphoma 4 %. Antinori, in 1630 autopsies, found 297 invasive fungal infections; 54.2 % of them were not suspected clinically.

Now we will look at the aim and design of the Brazilian study. This is a retrospective study in which consecutive autopsies of HIV-positive patients were studied. The patients had been in hospital for at least 24 hours, and the study was conducted in the Brazilian city of Uberaba in 1989-2008. The aim was to describe CNS changes according to antiretroviral therapy, to assess length of survival and to establish whether significant changes were suspected clinically. From 1989, in all autopsies, blood was systematically taken for HIV testing.

A standard is set for CNS histological samples: at least three tissue blocks are taken. The first block is prepared from different parts, the second from the basal ganglia and hippocampus, and the third from the midbrain, pons and cerebellum. When there were macroscopic changes, additional blocks were taken. Paraffin sections 5 µm thick were stained with haematoxylin and eosin.

The main stain was haematoxylin and eosin, and in addition special stains were also used. They are needed to assess microorganisms and demyelination. The methods used: Gram, Grocott, Mucicarmin, periodic acid-Schiff, that is, PAS, Fite Faraco and Luxol Fast Blue. For microorganisms Gram, Grocott, Mucicarmin, PAS and Fite Faraco were used, and for demyelination Luxol Fast Blue.

In some cases immunohistochemistry and in situ hybridisation were used. By the polymer method, monoclonal antibodies were used for toxoplasma, cytomegalovirus, herpes virus and JC virus. To characterise lymphoma, CD3, CD20, CD30, CD45 and CD45-LCA were used. In situ hybridisation for Epstein-Barr virus was carried out in three non-Hodgkin lymphomas.

The patients were divided into three groups according to antiretroviral therapy. Group A consisted of those who had taken no antiretroviral drugs. Group B included those who had received 1-2 antiretroviral drugs or HAART for less than 3 months, and also those who had stopped HAART for more than 2 months. Group C were those who had taken HAART for 3 months or more.

The sample was formed in stages. In 1989-2008, 1785 autopsies were carried out, of which 299, that is, 16.7 %, were HIV-seropositive. Then 15 were excluded: 9 lacked AIDS criteria, and 6 had no CNS histological section or case history. As a result, 284 autopsies were analysed.

We turn to the characteristics of the patients. Of the 284, 80, that is, 28.2 %, were women; the proportion of women rose from 17.8 % in 1989-1996 to 33 % in 1997-2008. The mean age was 35.7 ± 10.8 years, in the range from 16 to 69. Among risk factors, drug addiction was 33.1 %, that is, 94/284, and homosexuality or bisexuality 14.1 %. In 27.1 % of cases no risk factor was stated.

By treatment status, group A had 163 cases, that is, 57.4 %, group B 76 cases, that is, 26.8 %, and group C only 45 cases, that is, 15.8 %. In 69 cases, that is, 24.3 %, the diagnosis of HIV was made at autopsy or during hospitalisation in the hospital where death occurred. In all 18 cases in which the diagnosis was made only after death, an opportunistic infection was found in the CNS or other organs.

In 165 of 284 cases, that is, 58.1 %, significant changes of the CNS were identified. Infectious changes, with 54.2 %, far outnumber tumours, that is, 2.5 %, and vascular changes, that is, 1.1 %. Insignificant changes were found in 103 cases, that is, 36.3 %. Only in 16 cases, that is, 5.6 %, was the brain entirely normal.

The frequency of infections is given in the table. Toxoplasmosis was the most frequent infection and accounted for 85 cases, that is, 29.9 %; cryptococcosis follows with 45 cases, that is, 15.8 %. Purulent bacterial infection occurred in 11 cases, that is, 3.9 %, HIV encephalitis in 8 cases, that is, 2.8 %, and cytomegalovirus infection in 7 cases, that is, 2.5 %.

Non-infectious significant changes were found in 10 cases, that is, 3.5 %: 7 cases, that is, 2.5 %, were a primary CNS tumour and 3 cases, that is, 1.1 %, a vascular change. Among tumours there are 2 benign meningiomas, WHO grade I, and 5 lymphoid malignant tumours, including 4 cases, that is, 1.4 %, of diffuse B-cell non-Hodgkin lymphoma. Epstein-Barr virus was found in the lymphoma in all 3 cases examined. The vascular changes were three cases: subarachnoid haemorrhage in the brainstem, acute subdural haematoma and extensive intraparenchymal haemorrhage.

There was no overall difference in the frequency of changes between the groups. But compared with group A, in group C toxoplasmosis was less frequent and HIV encephalitis more frequent. Toxoplasmosis was 17.8 % in group C and 36.2 % in group A. HIV encephalitis was 11.1 % in group C and 1.8 % in group A.

Length of survival was established in 261 cases, that is, 90.9 %; in comparing the groups P < 0.001. In group C the mean survival was 49.1 months. This is more than four times the 11.2 months in group A, and almost twice as long as the 25.8 months in group B. That is, as the duration of therapy increases, the length of survival also increases.

t: Frequency of significant changes and HAART
n: Significant CNS changes were 63.8 % in group A and 48.7 % and 53.3 % in the other groups; this difference is not statistically significant. This may give the false impression that HAART does not change the prognosis. In fact, the benefit of therapy is clearly shown by length of survival. Remember: at the final stage the cause of death is often neuropathological changes.

t: Agreement between clinical suspicion and autopsy
n: In 91 of the 165 cases in which significant changes were found in the CNS, that is, 55.1 %, the clinical suspicion and the autopsy result did not agree; this makes up 32 % of the 284. Of these, 49, that is, 53.8 %, were type 1 discrepancy: a significant change was not identified during life, which could have changed the prognosis. All lymphoma cases fell into this type.

t: Types of discrepancy according to Goldman
n: According to Goldman, the types of discrepancy are divided into three. In type 1 there is a significant disease which, if identified during life, could have changed the prognosis. In type 2 a significant disease was not identified, but even if identified the prognosis would not have changed. In type 3 an insignificant disease was not identified, and its effect on prognosis is doubtful or absent.

t: Type 2 and 3 discrepancies; trend in type 1
n: Type 2 accounted for 22 cases, that is, 24.2 %; this was mostly cerebral toxoplasmosis in people who died of a pulmonary infection caused by another agent. Type 3 was 20 cases, that is, 22 %: for example, a meningioma in a patient with respiratory failure from Pneumocystis pneumonia. The type 1 error was 62.2 % before 1996, that is, 23/37, and then fell to 48.8 %, that is, 26/54. This was owing to the knowledge gained from the weekly anatomo-clinical conferences.

By prevalence of agents, viral infections made up only 6.7 % of the 284 cases. Protozoa, fungi and bacteria made up 49.3 %. HIV encephalitis was 2.8 %, cytomegalovirus 2.5 %, and JC virus infection 0.3 %. The reason is that patients usually present at the late stage of AIDS, and there is not enough time for HIV neuropathological changes to develop.

Cryptococcosis in Brazil was 15.8 %, and in the HAART group 15.6 %. In studies from developed countries, in the corresponding groups, this figure is from 0 to 5.6 %. The differences are probably related to environmental, geographical and socio-economic factors. That is, the prevalence of infections differs by region.

The conclusions of the Brazilian study are three. First: despite HAART, CNS changes are frequent in AIDS patients and remain an important cause of death. Second: in the HAART group the median length of survival is four times longer than in those without therapy. Third: in 55.1 % of cases autopsy and clinical diagnosis did not agree; this shows the importance of autopsy even with advanced diagnostics.

Now we turn to the South African study. The participants were adults with CD4 ≤150 cells/µL, not receiving TB treatment or ART, followed in primary health care clinics. All participants were followed for at least six months. If news of a death was received in good time, MIA was performed with the family's permission. The aim was to determine the autopsy prevalence of TB and other infections in adults followed in primary clinics.

In the MIA protocol, biopsies were taken from four organs: liver, spleen, and the right and left lung. At least five samples about 2 cm long were taken from one site, using an 18 gauge needle. The samples were intended for bacterial and fungal microscopy and culture, mycobacterial culture and histology. In addition, blood, cerebrospinal fluid, that is, CSF, urine and modified bronchoalveolar lavage, that is, BAL, were taken.

Attention was paid to the accuracy of MIA and to precautions. Ultrasound was used to examine liver changes and pleural fluid and to locate the spleen. The skin was cleaned with 70 % isopropyl alcohol and 10 % povidone-iodine. Wherever possible, MIA was performed by one operator with clinical training.

In the laboratory examination, all tissue samples, CSF, urine and BAL were cultured for mycobacteria by the MGIT method. Histology was carried out on all tissue samples. Ziehl-Neelsen, that is, ZN, staining detects mycobacteria, and Grocott staining detects fungi.

Experienced microbiologists determined for each deceased person which microorganism was an "artefact" and which a "pathogen". Enterococcus, Enterobacter, E. coli, Proteus, Bacillus, coagulase-negative staphylococci and Viridans streptococci were regarded as artefacts. Only Gram-negative microorganisms isolated from the spleen were taken as artefact, owing to the likelihood of contamination from abdominal organs. This means that every culture result went through the microbiologist's assessment.

On the MIA participants. From December 2012 to December 2014, 3022 people were enrolled, of whom 34 had MIA. 18, that is, 53 %, were women; median age 39 years; 25, that is, 74 %, died in hospital. The median CD4 at enrolment was 34 cells/µL. The median time from death to MIA was five days; 33/34, that is, 97 %, were carried out within 10 days.

We will consider the success of sampling. By histological assessment, lung biopsy was successful in 33/34, that is, 97 % of cases. Liver was successful in 30/34, that is, 88 %, and spleen in 21/34, that is, 62 % of cases. BAL was successfully obtained in 30/31, that is, 97 %, and CSF in 30/32, that is, 94 % of cases. The lowest success was observed in spleen biopsy.

By autopsy findings, signs of TB were found in 16/34, that is, 47 % of the deceased; in 14/16, that is, 88 %, there was extrapulmonary tuberculosis. Methods of detection: histology in 12 cases, that is, 75 %, culture in 11 cases, that is, 69 %, Xpert MTB/RIF in 5 cases, that is, 31 %. Histology and bacteriology together detected it in 8 cases, that is, 50 %. Of the 16 people with a sign of TB, 6, that is, 38 %, were not on TB treatment during life.

t: Tuberculosis: details by histology and culture
n: Details on tuberculosis. Of the 12 histological TB cases, in 4, that is, 33 %, it was found in lung, liver and spleen; in 2, that is, 17 %, in lung and liver; in another 2, that is, 17 %, in liver and spleen; in 2, that is, 17 %, in the lung only. By culture, the highest yield was from BAL, that is, 7 positive; from CSF and spleen 5 each; from lung and liver 4 each. Of 164 mycobacterial cultures, 37, that is, 23 %, were positive, and 13, that is, 8 %, were not interpreted because of bacterial contamination.

The description of the histological images is as follows. In the lung, a necrotising intra-alveolar granuloma and cytomegalovirus nuclear inclusions are seen with H&E staining; acid-fast bacilli are found with ZN. In the liver, a mycobacterial granuloma with H&E; in the lung, pleomorphic cryptococcal yeasts with Grocott. In the lung, small crescent-shaped cells of Pneumocystis jirovecii with Grocott, and in the liver active hepatitis B virus infection with H&E.

We turn to other mycobacteria and bacteria. Non-tuberculous mycobacteria, that is, NTM, were found in 3 cases, that is, 9 %: Mycobacterium avium in two, and Mycobacterium intracellulare in one. Pathogenic bacterial infection by culture was identified in 23/34, that is, 68 %; of these, in 14/23, that is, 61 %, there was Klebsiella spp. Of 33 lung histologies, 11, that is, 33 %, showed signs of bacterial pneumonia.

Cryptococcosis occurred in 4/34, that is, 12 % of cases; in 3 cases, that is, 75 %, there was histological confirmation, and Cryptococcus neoformans was cultured in 2 cases, that is, 50 %. Cytomegalovirus disease was found by histology in 2 cases, that is, 6 %, and in both it was disseminated. Pneumocystis pneumonia was also identified in 2 cases, that is, 6 %.

Co-occurrence of several pathogens is widespread. In 20 deceased, that is, 59 %, at least two infections were identified by histology or culture. Of the 16 people with a sign of TB, 9, that is, 56 %, also had bacterial disease, and 2, that is, 13 %, cryptococcosis. Of the 23 people with bacterial infection, 3, that is, 13 %, had cryptococcosis and 2, that is, 9 %, cytomegalovirus.

t: Additional findings in the liver and kidney
n: Additional findings in the liver and kidney. Of the 30 liver samples taken for histology, in 18, that is, 60 %, there is inflammation; steatosis in 12/18, that is, 67 %. Of the 18 with inflammation, in 5, that is, 28 %, there was acute or chronic hepatitis, of which four were considered viral. In the kidney, of 13 samples, in 6, that is, 46 %, interstitial nephritis and/or acute tubular necrosis were found.

Care is needed in interpreting autopsy results. Mycobacterium tuberculosis can remain alive for years after death and after storage in formalin. If a long time has passed between death and autopsy, autolysis and the possibility of microorganisms passing into other cavities increase. Therefore microbiological results, mycobacterial ones included, should be considered together with the clinical history and, ideally, histology.

t: The place of MIA in surveillance
n: On the place of MIA in surveillance. Respiratory samples, that is, BAL and lung tissue, give the highest yield for the diagnosis of TB. BAL Xpert MTB/RIF and BAL culture detected 9 TB cases; lung culture added another 2, and lung histology another 3. These three together accounted for 88 % of TB in the deceased.
